title: Do the missing voices of Renaissance songs survive in lute arrangements?
short: Printers sold each voice of a song in a separate book. Where only one part survives, a lute player’s arrangement might let us hear the voices together again.
matters: A lute player could play several parts on one instrument, writing down where to put the fingers on its strings. These books of fingerings, called tablatures, can preserve a version of a song whose singers’ books are now incomplete.
stuck: Royston Gustavson and David Fallows rediscovered a tenor book in Bern from a set Christian Egenolff printed in 1536. ReRenaissance and the RISM Digital Center brought nine pieces to recording in 2025. A lute arrangement might preserve additional notes, but players also added ornaments, left out voices and changed harmonies.
solved: Match several distinctive phrases from the surviving vocal line in order, then have a reader compare the entire arrangement with the tenor and other surviving sources. Credit the result as a historical arrangement. Attribute a particular note to a lost vocal part only where another witness supports it.
approach: Begin with songs that survive both in vocal partbooks and in dated lute tablatures. Hide the titles and test how often the search recovers the known arrangements.
Search for phrases from the Bern tenor in other tablatures, allowing for transposition, added notes and changed titles. Compare early collections with arrangements made after 1536.
Publish the two readings side by side so musicians can see which notes survive, which the arranger supplied and which a modern performance reconstructs.
